steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper on training-efficient video foundation models, where an image foundation model acts as an "unmasked teacher" for masked video pre-training. Motivate the problem, explain where existing approaches fall short, introduce the method and its training framework, and summarize the main results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Video understanding and the limits of image foundation models
- Challenges of building VFMs on top of IFMs
- VideoMAE: data-efficient but costly
- Our method: Unmasked Teacher (UMT)
- Progressive two-stage pre-training framework
- Experiments, results and training cost

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Video understanding and the limits of IFMs
  - critical skill for AI systems analyzing videos
  - progress driven by Image Foundation Models (IFMs) (cite): trained on massive data, adapted to downstream tasks (cite)
  - IFMs focus on scenes/objects, ignore motion patterns and object interactions
  - true Video Foundation Models (VFMs) underexplored: high compute cost, data scarcity
- Building VFMs on IFMs: challenges
  - reduces training cost, but image -> video knowledge transfer is hard
  - limited video data + domain gap: post-pretraining may undermine IFM generality (cite)
  - strong spatial init = shortcut, perceive video from scenes in single frames (“grass” in “horse riding”); can't learn spatiotemporal relations for temporal actions (“opening”/“closing”, Figure 2)
  - hard to scale: needs well-prepared IFMs
- VideoMAE (cite)
  - data-efficient spatiotemporal features from scratch; strong on temporal action recognition/detection
  - cost: long pre-training (2400 epochs on 160k videos)
  - low-level pixel reconstruction conflicts with high-level cross-modal alignment (cite) -> bad for video-language
  - extra decoder for masked + unmasked tokens -> memory cost from global self-attention, hard to scale
- Our method: UnMasked Teacher (UMT)
  - training-efficient method for temporal-sensitive VFMs, combine benefits of previous methods
  - don't adapt public IFM like CLIP (cite) directly; use it as teacher to train vanilla ViT from scratch
  - mask most video tokens (low semantics), align unmasked tokens to teacher's via linear projection
  - keeps VideoMAE's data efficiency + multimodal-friendly encoder (Table 1)
  - no decoder, only unmasked tokens -> less GPU memory than VideoMAE; teacher semantics -> faster convergence
  - handles scene-related (cite) and temporal-related actions (cite); CLIP alignment -> cross-modal compatible
- Progressive pre-training (Figure 2)
  - Stage 1: video data only, masked video modeling -> strong on video-only tasks
  - Stage 2: public vision-language data, multi-modality learning -> video-text retrieval (cite), video QA (cite)
  - UMT in both stages: fewer training sources, faster convergence
  - readily-available image and language foundation models (cite) -> easily scalable
- Experiments
  - public data/models only (Figure 1), state of the art on many tasks
  - action recognition (cite): 90.6% top-1 on K400; spatiotemporal localization (cite): 39.8 mAP on AVA
  - video-text retrieval (cite): 58.8 R@1 on MSRVTT; video QA (cite): 47.1% on MSRVTT
  - vs CoCa (cite): 2,048 CloudTPUv4 chips for 5 days; ours: 32 A100(80G) GPUs within 6 days -> 70 \times less carbon

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Video understanding has become an important skill for artificial intelligence systems that need to analyze and understand videos. Right now, progress in video understanding mostly comes from Image Foundation Models (IFMs), which are trained on massive datasets and then adapted to different downstream tasks. But IFMs focus more on scenes and objects, and they disregard the motion patterns and object interactions that complex video understanding needs. True Video Foundation Models (VFMs) are still underexplored, because the computational costs are high and there is not much data.

Building VFMs on top of well-learned IFMs reduces the training costs, but transferring the knowledge from the image domain to the video domain is hard. First, video data is limited and there is a big domain gap, so video post-pretraining may undermine the generality that was inherited from the IFMs. Second, the strong spatial initialization gives the model a shortcut where it perceives videos from the scenes in single frames (e.g., “grass” in “horse riding”). This constrains VFMs from learning spatiotemporal relationships, which are needed to recognize and localize temporal-related actions like “opening” and “closing” in Figure 2. Third, this paradigm is hard to scale up because it needs well-prepared IFMs.

VideoMAE was recently successful and it gives a data-efficient way to learn good spatiotemporal features from scratch, and it handles complex temporal action recognition and detection tasks very well. However, the data efficiency and the spatiotemporal modeling come at the cost of long pre-training (e.g., 2400 epochs on 160k videos). It is also not a good fit for video-language tasks, because the low-level pixel reconstruction task conflicts with high-level cross-modal alignment. On top of that, the extra decoder that handles masked and unmasked tokens has high memory costs because of global self-attention, so scaling up this paradigm is also hard.

- Our method: UnMasked Teacher (UMT)
  - training-efficient method for temporal-sensitive VFMs, combining benefits of previous methods
  - don't adapt public IFM like CLIP directly; use it as teacher to train vanilla ViT from scratch
  - mask most video tokens (low semantics), align unmasked ones to the teacher's with linear projection
  - data efficiency of VideoMAE + multimodal-friendly encoder (Table 1)
  - no decoder -> less GPU memory than VideoMAE; teacher -> faster convergence
  - good on scene-related and temporal-related actions; CLIP alignment -> cross-modal learning
- Progressive pre-training (Figure 2)
  - Stage 1: video only, masked video modeling -> video-only tasks
  - Stage 2: public vision-language data -> video-text retrieval, video QA
  - UMT in both stages; readily-available image/language foundation models -> scalable
- Experiments
  - public sources only (Figure 1); SOTA on action recognition (90.6% top-1 K400), localization (39.8 mAP AVA), retrieval (58.8 R@1 MSRVTT), QA (47.1% MSRVTT)
  - CoCa: 2,048 CloudTPUv4 chips for 5 days vs ours 32 A100(80G) GPUs within 6 days -> 70 \times less carbon

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Video understanding has become an important skill for artificial intelligence systems that need to analyze and understand videos. Right now, progress in video understanding mostly comes from Image Foundation Models (IFMs), which are trained on massive datasets and then adapted to different downstream tasks. But IFMs focus more on scenes and objects, and they disregard the motion patterns and object interactions that complex video understanding needs. True Video Foundation Models (VFMs) are still underexplored, because the computational costs are high and there is not much data.

Building VFMs on top of well-learned IFMs reduces the training costs, but transferring the knowledge from the image domain to the video domain is hard. First, video data is limited and there is a big domain gap, so video post-pretraining may undermine the generality that was inherited from the IFMs. Second, the strong spatial initialization gives the model a shortcut where it perceives videos from the scenes in single frames (e.g., “grass” in “horse riding”). This constrains VFMs from learning spatiotemporal relationships, which are needed to recognize and localize temporal-related actions like “opening” and “closing” in Figure 2. Third, this paradigm is hard to scale up because it needs well-prepared IFMs.

VideoMAE was recently successful and it gives a data-efficient way to learn good spatiotemporal features from scratch, and it handles complex temporal action recognition and detection tasks very well. However, the data efficiency and the spatiotemporal modeling come at the cost of long pre-training (e.g., 2400 epochs on 160k videos). It is also not a good fit for video-language tasks, because the low-level pixel reconstruction task conflicts with high-level cross-modal alignment. On top of that, the extra decoder that handles masked and unmasked tokens has high memory costs because of global self-attention, so scaling up this paradigm is also hard.

In this paper we present a training-efficient method for temporal-sensitive VFMs that combines the benefits of the previous methods. We do not directly adapt a public IFM such as CLIP. Instead we use it as an UnMasked Teacher (UMT) to train a vanilla ViT from scratch. We mask out most of the video tokens, the ones with low semantics, and we only align the unmasked tokens with a linear projection to the corresponding tokens from the teacher. This way the approach inherits the data efficiency of VideoMAE, and it also makes the learned video encoder multimodal-friendly (validated in Table 1). Also, since we train with only the unmasked tokens and without a decoder, we save GPU memory compared to VideoMAE, and the teacher’s semantically rich representation guides the model so it converges faster. The resulting model handles both scene-related and temporal-related actions very well, and because it is aligned to CLIP features it is compatible with cross-modal learning.

We propose a progressive pre-training framework (Figure 2) to handle different video tasks. Stage 1 uses only video data for masked video modeling, and the model we get is good at video-only tasks. Stage 2 uses public vision-language data for multi-modality learning. With this the model can do complex video-language tasks like video-text retrieval and video question answering. UMT is used in both stages, which reduces the training sources a lot and speeds up convergence. Because image and language foundation models are readily available, our simple framework can easily be scaled for video foundation models.

We do a lot of experiments to check how effective and efficient our approach is. Figure 1 shows that, using public sources (data/models) for pre-training, our method gets state-of-the-art performance on various video tasks: action recognition (90.6% top-1 accuracy on K400), spatiotemporal localization (39.8 mAP on AVA), video-text retrieval (58.8 R@1 on MSRVTT) and video question-answering (47.1% accuracy on MSRVTT). Our method is also much more environmentally friendly than CoCa, which uses 2,048 CloudTPUv4 chips for 5 days. Our pre-training needs 32 A100(80G) GPUs within 6 days, which means a 70 \times reduction in carbon emissions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Video understanding has emerged as a critical skill for artificial intelligence systems to analyze and comprehend videos. Progress in video understanding is currently driven by Image Foundation Models (IFMs) [5,6,7,3], which are trained on massive datasets and adapted for different downstream tasks [8,9,10,11]. However, IFMs tend to focus on scenes and objects, disregarding the essential motion patterns and object interactions required for complex video understanding. True Video Foundation Models (VFMs) remain underexplored due to high computational costs and data scarcity.

While building VFMs on well-learned IFMs reduces training costs, it makes transferring knowledge from the image domain to the video domain challenging. Firstly, due to limited video data and a substantial domain gap, video post-pretraining may undermine the generality inherited from IFMs [12]. Moreover, the strong spatial initialization offers a shortcut to perceive videos from the scenes in single frames (e.g., “grass” in “horse riding”), which keeps VFMs from learning the spatiotemporal relationships needed to recognize and localize temporal-related actions, such as “opening” and “closing” in Figure 2. Lastly, this paradigm is difficult to scale up, since it requires well-prepared IFMs.

The recent success of VideoMAE [13,14] offers a data-efficient way to learn effective spatiotemporal features from scratch, and it handles complex temporal action recognition and detection tasks impressively. Nonetheless, its data efficiency and spatiotemporal modeling come at the price of long pre-training (e.g., 2400 epochs on 160k videos). Besides, it is not well-suited for video-language tasks, since low-level pixel reconstruction conflicts with high-level cross-modal alignment [15]. Additionally, the extra decoder that handles masked and unmasked tokens causes high memory costs due to global self-attention, which also makes this paradigm hard to scale up.

In this paper, we present a training-efficient method for temporal-sensitive VFMs that integrates the benefits of previous methods. Rather than directly adapting a public IFM, e.g., CLIP [3], we use it as an UnMasked Teacher (UMT) to train a vanilla ViT from scratch. We mask out most of the video tokens with low semantics and only align the unmasked tokens, via a linear projection, to the corresponding ones from the teacher. This approach not only inherits the data efficiency of VideoMAE but also makes the learned video encoder multimodal-friendly (validated in Table 1). Moreover, training with only unmasked tokens and no decoder saves further GPU memory compared to VideoMAE, while the teacher’s semantically rich representation leads to faster convergence. Notably, the resulting model handles both scene-related [16,17] and temporal-related actions [18,19] exceptionally well, and the alignment to CLIP features makes it compatible with cross-modal learning.

To address various video tasks, we propose the progressive pre-training framework in Figure 2. In Stage 1, we use only video data for masked video modeling, which results in a model that excels at video-only tasks. In Stage 2, we employ public vision-language data for multi-modality learning, allowing the model to conduct complex video-language tasks such as video-text retrieval [20,21] and video question answering [22,23]. We use UMT in both stages, which significantly reduces the training sources and speeds up convergence. Thanks to readily-available image and language foundation models [3,24,25,26,27], our simple framework is easily scalable for video foundation models.

We conduct extensive experiments to verify the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach. As shown in Figure 1, with public sources (data/models) for pre-training, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on various video tasks, including action recognition [16,28,29,17,18] (90.6% top-1 accuracy on K400), spatiotemporal localization [19] (39.8 mAP on AVA), video-text retrieval [20,30,31,21,32] (58.8 R@1 on MSRVTT) and video question-answering [22,23,33] (47.1% accuracy on MSRVTT). Our method is also much more environmentally friendly than CoCa [4], which uses 2,048 CloudTPUv4 chips for 5 days. In contrast, our pre-training requires 32 A100(80G) GPUs within 6 days, a 70 \times reduction in carbon emissions.

Learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision. In International Conference on Machine Learning , 2021.
[4] Jiahui Yu, Zirui Wang, Vijay Vasudevan, Legg Yeung, Mojtaba Seyedhosseini, and Yonghui Wu. Coca: Contrastive captioners are image-text foundation models. Transactions on Machine Learning Research , 2022.
